title: He Has Risen: The Empty Tomb
summary: Early on the first day of the week three women come to anoint Jesus' body and find the great stone rolled away. A young man in white tells them that Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified, has risen, and sends them to tell the disciples and Peter that he is going ahead of them into Galilee; they flee in fear and say nothing to anyone. Verses 9 to 20, absent from the earliest manuscripts, describe appearances of the risen Jesus, his commission to preach the gospel to all creation, and his ascension.
story: Mark's story ends where it has been heading since the first passion prediction: after three days he will rise. The women who watched the crucifixion and the burial are the first to hear the news, and the message they receive restores the disciples who fled, naming Peter, who denied Jesus, in particular. The promise that Jesus goes ahead of them into Galilee fulfills his word at the Last Supper (14:28) and points them back to where the story began, now to follow him again. Whether the book originally ended at verse 8 or not, the resurrection is not a coda to Mark's Gospel but its goal. Acts and the letters of the New Testament are what happened when the disciples went.
historical:
The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday, and the women bought spices then so they could go to the tomb at first light on Sunday, the first day of the week. That day became the day of Christian worship because of what happened on it. The women are named, and the named witnesses matter. In the ancient world women's testimony carried less weight than men's in many settings, and many historians note that a story invented to persuade would hardly have made women the first witnesses. All four Gospels agree that they were.

The ending of Mark raises a question of textual history, the study of how the New Testament was copied and handed down. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the Greek New Testament, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both from the fourth century, end the book at 16:8. The church fathers Eusebius and Jerome, in the fourth century, reported that the most accurate copies they knew ended there. Most later manuscripts contain verses 9 to 20, the longer ending, and it was known by the late second century, since Irenaeus quotes verse 19 as Mark's. One Old Latin manuscript (Codex Bobiensis) has only a short ending of a sentence or two instead, several Greek manuscripts have both, and one fifth-century manuscript (Codex Washingtonianus) adds a further saying after verse 14.
cultural:
Jews did not embalm the dead as Egyptians did, but they washed the body, wrapped it in cloth, and applied spices and perfumed oils as an act of love and to lessen the odor of decay. The women came expecting a corpse. Wealthy families' tombs were cut into rock, with a low entrance closed by a large stone that could be rolled or pushed into place, and inside was a bench or niche where the body was laid. The young man dressed in white sitting on the right is presented as an angelic messenger; white clothing signals heavenly origin, as at the transfiguration (9:3), and the right side was the place of honor and favorable news.

Fear, trembling, and amazement are the normal human response in Scripture to God's direct action, not a sign of unbelief alone. The Greek of verse 8 ends with the small word for, an unusual way to end a sentence and, if it is the end, a book. Such endings are rare but not unknown in Greek writing.
literary: Verses 1 to 8 are brief and carefully built. The women's question about the stone (verse 3) is answered before they arrive. The angel's words reverse the story's darkness: the one who was crucified has been raised, the place where they laid him is empty, and the disciples, including Peter, are summoned back. The last line is startling: they said nothing to anyone because they were afraid. Throughout Mark people told to be silent have spoken; now people told to speak are silent. Readers who think Mark ended here see an intentional ending that leaves the reader to answer the call the women failed to carry out, trusting that the promise of Galilee will be kept (as the existence of the Gospel itself shows it was). Others find such an ending too abrupt for any ancient book and conclude that the original last page was lost or never written. Verses 9 to 20 differ from the rest of Mark in vocabulary and style and gather material also found in other books: the appearance to Mary Magdalene (John 20), the two on the road (Luke 24), the great commission (Matthew 28), tongues (Acts 2), and a snakebite survived (Acts 28:3-6).

outline.t: The women at the empty tomb
Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene (longer ending)
Jesus appears to two in the country
Jesus appears to the Eleven and sends them out
The ascension and the disciples' preaching

doctrines.note: The church confesses, as a first-order article of faith, that Jesus was bodily raised from the dead on the third day. The tomb is empty and the place where they laid him is shown; the one who was crucified is the one who is risen. This is not a metaphor for his influence or the disciples' renewed courage but an event, the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to all who belong to him.

The resurrection vindicates everything Jesus claimed. He had said three times that the Son of Man would rise after three days, and before the high priest that he would be seen at the right hand of Power. God's raising him is the Father's verdict on the Son whom the world condemned.

The angel sends the women to tell the disciples, and in the longer ending the risen Jesus sends the Eleven to preach the gospel to all creation. The story of Jesus does not end with his followers watching; it continues in their going and telling.

The message goes to the disciples and Peter, all of whom fled and one of whom denied him with curses. The resurrection brings restoration to failed followers. The way back is opened by the risen Lord himself, who goes ahead of them.

words.note: Egeiro, to raise or to rise, used of waking from sleep, getting up, and rising from the dead. The angel's announcement uses the passive form, he has been raised, a way of pointing to God as the one who acted. The same verb described Jesus raising Jairus's daughter and lifting the boy who seemed dead (5:41, 9:27).

Proago, to go before or lead the way. Jesus went ahead of his disciples on the road to Jerusalem (10:32), and now he goes ahead of them into Galilee. The risen Lord does not wait for his followers to find their way back; he leads them.

Tromos, trembling, often joined in Scripture with fear as the response to God's power. The women's trembling and amazement at the tomb place them in the long line of those who have met the living God and been undone by it.

Apisteo, to refuse to believe. In the longer ending it describes the disciples who would not believe Mary Magdalene's report that Jesus was alive (verse 11), and then anyone who will not believe the gospel (verse 16); verse 14 uses the related noun for the Eleven's unbelief. The early church did not hide the fact that its first leaders doubted, and the risen Jesus rebukes their hardness of heart before he sends them.

christ: The chapter shows that the crucified Jesus is alive. The angel's words hold the two together: Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified, has risen. His death was real, and so is his resurrection, and the church has always confessed his bodily resurrection as the event on which its faith stands or falls (1 Corinthians 15:14-17). The resurrection shows that Jesus is who Mark said he was from the first line, the Christ and the Son of God, and that his death was not defeat but the ransom he came to give. In the longer ending he is taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, the place Psalm 110 promised the Messiah and that Jesus himself claimed before the high priest. From there he works with his people as they preach, which is the story Acts goes on to tell.

hard.q: Did Mark's Gospel originally end at 16:8, and how should readers treat verses 9 to 20?
hard.a: The evidence is set out in the notes above. In summary, the earliest complete manuscripts and the testimony of Eusebius and Jerome support an ending at verse 8, while the longer ending is found in the great majority of later manuscripts and was known to Irenaeus in the late second century. Its vocabulary and style differ noticeably from the rest of Mark, and its content largely gathers what is reported in the other Gospels and Acts. On this basis most textual scholars, including many who hold a high view of Scripture's inspiration, conclude that verses 9 to 20 were added early by another hand. A minority defends the longer ending as original, arguing from its wide attestation in later manuscripts, its early use in the church, and the difficulty of a book ending with the word for. Among those who think it was added, some believe Mark deliberately ended at verse 8, and others think his original ending was lost. Most modern Bibles print verses 9 to 20 with a note or in brackets. Readers can treat the passage as an ancient and valuable witness to how the early church summarized the resurrection appearances, while building no doctrine or practice on it alone. This matters especially for verse 18: a small number of churches have practiced handling snakes and drinking poison on its basis, which is to build on a disputed text and, in Jesus' own words elsewhere, to put God to the test (Matthew 4:7). The resurrection itself does not depend on these verses; verses 1 to 8 proclaim it plainly.

questions: The angel sent the message to the disciples and Peter. What does it mean to you that Peter, after his denial, is named for restoration?
The women were afraid and said nothing. What makes you hesitate to speak about the risen Jesus, and what might it look like to speak anyway?
Jesus goes ahead of his disciples into Galilee, back to where they first followed him. Where might the risen Jesus be calling you to begin following him again?
